chapter_title: Ensuring Data Plane Continuity: NSF and Aggregated Ethernet (LAG)
chapter_summary:
While GRES and NSR are crucial for maintaining control plane continuity, they don't directly address the data plane's ability to forward traffic during a failure. This is where Nonstop Forwarding (NSF) comes into play, working in concert with GRES and NSR to provide a truly robust, end-to-end high availability solution. NSF ensures that the data plane, which is responsible for the actual forwarding of packets, continues to operate even if the control plane experiences a temporary disruption, such as a Routing Engine switchover.

Nonstop Forwarding (NSF) allows the Packet Forwarding Engine (PFE) to continue forwarding traffic using its last-known forwarding table entries, even when the Routing Engine (RE) becomes unavailable or is undergoing a switchover. The PFEs are intelligent enough to hold onto their forwarding state for a grace period, typically while the new primary RE is coming online and NSR is re-establishing routing protocol adjacencies. This prevents traffic blackholing during the brief period when the control plane might be transitioning. Without NSF, a Routing Engine switchover could cause the PFEs to flush their forwarding tables, leading to significant traffic loss until the new primary RE fully converges.

The interaction between GRES, NSR, and NSF is critical for comprehensive HA. GRES ensures the kernel and interface state continuity. NSR ensures routing protocol state continuity. NSF ensures that the data plane continues to forward traffic based on the existing forwarding information during the control plane transition. Together, these three features create a powerful synergy:
1.  **GRES:** The backup RE takes over quickly, maintaining the core OS and hardware state.
2.  **NSR:** The routing protocols (e.g., OSPF, BGP) on the new master RE immediately resume operation with synchronized state, preventing session drops.
3.  **NSF:** The PFEs continue forwarding traffic based on the last known good routes, bridging the gap until the new master RE and NSR fully stabilize and push any necessary updates to the forwarding tables.

Configuring NSF is typically done on a per-protocol basis, although it's often enabled by default or implicitly with NSR for many protocols. For example, for OSPF, you might configure `graceful-restart` which enables NSF capabilities for OSPF. For BGP, it's configured under `[edit protocols bgp graceful-restart]`.

```junos
# Example for OSPF graceful restart (enables NSF capabilities for OSPF)
set protocols ospf graceful-restart

# Example for BGP graceful restart (enables NSF capabilities for BGP)
set protocols bgp graceful-restart
```

While NSF handles control plane disruptions, what about failures at the physical link layer? This is where Aggregated Ethernet (AE), also known as Link Aggregation Group (LAG) or EtherChannel, provides crucial data plane redundancy and load balancing. Aggregated Ethernet allows you to bundle multiple physical Ethernet links into a single logical interface. This logical interface then appears as a single, higher-bandwidth link to the network.

The primary benefits of AE are:
*   **Link Redundancy:** If one physical link within the bundle fails, the remaining links continue to carry traffic, and the logical AE interface remains up. This prevents a complete outage due to a single cable or port failure.
*   **Increased Bandwidth:** The total bandwidth of the AE interface is the sum of the bandwidths of its active member links, providing higher throughput.
*   **Load Balancing:** Traffic is distributed across the active member links, utilizing the available bandwidth more efficiently. Junos OS offers various load-balancing options based on source/destination MAC, IP, or port information.

Configuring Aggregated Ethernet involves defining the AE interface and then adding physical Ethernet interfaces as members. You also typically configure Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) to automatically manage the bundle.

```junos
# Configure the aggregated Ethernet interface
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode trunk
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members all # or specific VLANs

# Configure LACP on the aggregated interface
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options minimum-links 1 # Or more, depending on desired redundancy

# Add physical interfaces to the bundle
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
```

A common mistake when configuring AE is not matching the LACP mode (active/passive) and load-balancing hashing algorithms on both ends of the link. Mismatched configurations can lead to the AE bundle not forming or traffic not being distributed as expected. Another pitfall is setting `minimum-links` too high, which could cause the entire bundle to go down if fewer links than specified are active, even if some links are still operational. Safety note: Always ensure that the physical interfaces intended for an AE bundle are not configured with other logical units or protocols before adding them to the bundle, as this can cause conflicts.

By combining NSF for control plane resilience with Aggregated Ethernet for physical link redundancy, you create a highly robust data plane that can withstand various types of failures, ensuring continuous traffic flow and meeting the stringent uptime requirements of modern enterprise networks.

screens.title: Ensuring Data Plane Continuity
screens.subtitle: How NSF and Aggregated Ethernet (AE/LAG) keep traffic flowing during failures

narration.text: In enterprise networks, keeping packets flowing is as important as maintaining routing state. In this lesson you will learn two complementary approaches: Nonstop Forwarding, which keeps the Packet Forwarding Engine forwarding during a control plane transition, and Aggregated Ethernet, which bundles physical links to prevent a single-cable outage from taking a logical link down. We’ll explain how NSF bridges a Routing Engine switchover by preserving forwarding entries on the PFE and how AE uses LACP to form resilient, higher-bandwidth logical interfaces. You’ll see configuration examples used in Junos OS and a practical lab scenario that builds an ae0 bundle with two member ports. I’ll highlight common mistakes to avoid, like mismatched LACP modes or setting minimum-links too high, and why combining NSF with GRES and NSR produces a strong end-to-end availability posture. By the end you’ll be able to describe when to enable NSF, how AE prevents data-plane interruptions from physical link failures, and what checks to run after you commit changes. Consider a production link that carries critical traffic: what single changes would you make to ensure minimal disruption? That question will guide our hands-on steps.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: NSF preserves forwarding during control-plane transitions while AE/LAG provides link-level redundancy and bandwidth aggregation; together they protect the data plane from both control-plane and physical failures.

screens.title: What is Nonstop Forwarding (NSF)?
screens.subtitle: How PFEs preserve forwarding during a control-plane switchover

narration.text: Nonstop Forwarding is a data-plane resilience feature that ensures a device continues forwarding packets using the Packet Forwarding Engine’s last-known forwarding table entries when the Routing Engine is temporarily unavailable. In practical terms, the PFE retains its forwarding state for a grace period while the backup Routing Engine takes over and NSR re-establishes protocol adjacencies. A concrete example is a master RE that fails and a backup takes over: with NSF enabled the PFE does not flush routes and thus avoids blackholing traffic while BGP or OSPF sessions are resynchronized. A common misconception is that NSF alone fixes routing convergence; it does not. NSF preserves forwarding state but relies on GRES to preserve kernel and interface state and on NSR to restore routing protocol sessions. If NSF is not enabled or supported for a protocol, the PFE could flush entries and drop traffic during switchover. Key signs that NSF is working are continuous traffic flow during an RE switchover and rapid restoration of protocol adjacencies after NSR completes. To check understanding: how would you explain the difference between NSF and NSR to a colleague who thinks they are the same feature?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: NSF lets PFEs forward packets using cached forwarding information while control-plane components recover.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is Nonstop Forwarding (NSF)?
Definition

NSF allows the PFE to keep forwarding packets using its last-known forwarding table while the Routing Engine is unavailable or switching over. The PFE holds state for a grace period to bridge the transition.

Why this matters

Without NSF, a switchover can cause the PFE to flush forwarding tables and create traffic loss until the new RE and NSR repopulate forwarding state.

Common misconception

NSF is not a routing protocol fix; it only preserves forwarding while NSR and the new RE restore protocol adjacencies.

Annotated example
Scenario

Primary RE fails and backup RE becomes primary. PFEs continue forwarding using cached routes while NSR reestablishes protocol sessions.

Verification
  • Observe continuous traffic during switchover.
  • Confirm routing adjacencies are reestablished by NSR after switchover.
  • Check device logs for graceful-restart messages for protocols.
Key takeaway
NSF reduces or eliminates traffic loss during RE transitions by letting PFEs forward on cached state until control-plane synchronization completes.

screens.title: How NSF, NSR, and GRES Work Together
screens.subtitle: A coordinated sequence during a Routing Engine switchover

narration.text: A switchover involves a coordinated sequence that keeps both the control plane and the data plane available. First, Graceful Routing Engine Switchover preserves the kernel and interface state so interfaces remain up and hardware state persists. Next, NSR synchronizes routing protocol state between the active and backup Routing Engines so protocols resume with minimal interruption. During this period, NSF lets the Packet Forwarding Engine continue forwarding based on its last-known forwarding table entries. A concrete sequence: the primary RE fails, GRES ensures the kernel remains intact while the backup assumes control, NSF prevents the PFE from flushing forwarding entries, and NSR restores BGP or OSPF adjacencies so the new RE can program the forwarding plane if necessary. A common misconception is thinking GRES or NSR alone will prevent data-plane loss; they are necessary but not sufficient. NSF is the specific mechanism that keeps forwarding alive. After this sequence completes, any delta updates are applied and normal operation resumes. How would you test each phase to confirm it completed successfully? That test plan guides both design and verification. How NSF, NSR, and GRES Work Together means gres preserves system state, nsr restores protocol adjacencies, and nsf keeps the pfe forwarding—together they deliver end-to-end resilience.. In practical terms, a coordinated sequence during a routing engine switchover. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sequence
keyIdea.text: GRES preserves system state, NSR restores protocol adjacencies, and NSF keeps the PFE forwarding—together they deliver end-to-end resilience.

content.html:
Process Flow › How NSF, NSR, and GRES Work Together
Coordinated sequence

During a Routing Engine switchover these features cooperate so traffic is not interrupted: GRES preserves system and interface state, NSR syncs routing protocols, and NSF keeps PFEs forwarding on cached entries until the control plane is fully restored.

Verification prompts
  • Confirm interface states remained up across switchover (GRES).
  • Check routing adjacencies reappear without full tear-down (NSR).
  • Observe no traffic blackholing during the transition (NSF).
1
GRES: preserve kernel/interface
Backup RE takes over without resetting kernel or interfaces.
2
NSR: protocol state sync
Routing protocols resume with synchronized state on the new master RE.
3
NSF: maintain forwarding
PFEs forward using last-known entries, bridging the time until NSR finishes.
Check your understanding
If NSR is not configured but NSF is, forwarding may persist briefly but routing adjacencies will not be synchronized, which can lead to stale route visibility. Full HA requires the three features working together.

screens.title: Enabling NSF per-protocol
screens.subtitle: OSPF and BGP examples in Junos OS

narration.text: NSF is typically enabled on a per-protocol basis. In Junos OS you enable graceful-restart for protocols such as OSPF and BGP to provide NSF capabilities for those protocols. For example, adding graceful-restart under OSPF signals neighbors to preserve adjacency state and allows the PFE to forward using existing entries while NSR resynchronizes. For BGP you configure graceful-restart under the BGP stanza. A concrete configuration example is provided in the course material: set protocols ospf graceful-restart and set protocols bgp graceful-restart. After committing these commands you should monitor neighbor messages for graceful-restart capability and confirm that traffic persists during a restart or switchover. A common mistake is assuming graceful-restart is automatic for every protocol; always verify protocol support and default behavior for your platform. As you practice, test in a lab by restarting an RE or simulating a switchover and observing that the PFE continues forwarding while adjacencies are restored. Enabling NSF per-protocol means enable graceful-restart for the routing protocols you need to support nsf functionality in the control plane.. In practical terms, ospf and bgp examples in junos os. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Enable graceful-restart for the routing protocols you need to support NSF functionality in the control plane.

content.html:
Configuration › Enabling NSF per-protocol
Concept

NSF is often provided by graceful-restart features of routing protocols. Enabling graceful-restart tells neighbors to preserve adjacencies and allows PFEs to keep forwarding while control-plane state is reestablished.

Common pitfall

Assuming all protocols automatically support NSF. Verify for each protocol and platform whether graceful-restart NSEF semantics are supported.

Code examples
set protocols ospf graceful-restart

set protocols bgp graceful-restart
After commit, watch neighbor messages and run verification commands during a controlled switchover to confirm forwarding continuity and adjacency restoration.

screens.title: Aggregated Ethernet (AE / LAG)
screens.subtitle: What AE provides: redundancy, bandwidth, and load balancing

narration.text: Aggregated Ethernet, also known as LAG or AE, bundles multiple physical Ethernet interfaces into a single logical interface. The logical interface presents combined bandwidth equal to the sum of active member links and remains up if at least the required minimum-links are present. A key use case is connecting an access or distribution switch to an upstream router where you need both higher throughput and resiliency to a single cable or port failure. AE also supports load balancing across member links, using hashing schemes based on source and destination MAC, IP, or transport ports to distribute flows. A common mistake is mismatching LACP modes or hashing configurations between devices; mismatches can prevent a bundle from forming or result in imbalanced traffic. Another pitfall is setting minimum-links higher than the number of physically available members, which can bring the whole bundle down even when some links remain operational. When you design an AE, choose member interfaces uniformly, enable LACP for automatic negotiation, and plan hashing according to traffic characteristics. How would you choose hashing criteria for many small TCP flows versus fewer large flows?

keyIdea.title: AE summary
keyIdea.text: AE combines multiple physical links into one logical interface to increase bandwidth and tolerate single-link failures while offering configurable load balancing.

content.html:
Definition › Aggregated Ethernet (AE / LAG)
AE explained

AE bundles multiple physical links into a single logical interface so the network sees one higher-bandwidth, resilient link. If a member link fails, traffic continues on remaining links and the logical interface stays up if minimum-links requirements are met.

Redundancy
Single-link failure does not drop the logical interface.
Bandwidth
Aggregate of active member link rates.
Load balancing
Traffic distributed using hash algorithms.
Design notes
  • Use uniform port speeds and types within a bundle.
  • Enable LACP for automatic and predictable bundle formation.
  • Match hashing and LACP mode on both ends to avoid formation issues.
Pitfall

Setting minimum-links too high can cause the bundle to go down even when some links remain active. Choose a safe minimum based on required redundancy.

screens.title: Configure Aggregated Ethernet (ae0) and LACP
screens.subtitle: Junos OS commands for bundle creation and member assignment

narration.text: Configuring an Aggregated Ethernet bundle in Junos OS involves defining the ae interface, enabling LACP, setting minimum-links, and assigning physical member interfaces to that bundle. The common commands include creating ae0, specifying its ethernet-switching properties, enabling lacp with active mode, and adding member ports with 802.3ad ether-options. For example, you define ae0, set interface-mode trunk for VLANs, enable lacp active, and set minimum-links to the desired redundancy level. Then you configure ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 to use ether-options 802.3ad ae0. After committing, verify the aggregated interface and LACP state. A practical mistake to avoid is configuring logical units on member ports before placing them into an AE; they must be free of conflicting configurations. In a lab, add the commands, commit, and immediately run show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces ae0 to confirm the bundle formed and traffic flows across both links. Configure Aggregated Ethernet (ae0) and LACP means define ae0, enable lacp, set minimum-links, and assign physical interfaces using ether-options 802.3ad.. Configuration › Configure Aggregated Ethernet (ae0) and LACP
Commands (example)

set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode trunk
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members all

# Configure LACP on the aggregated interface
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options minimum-links 1

# Add physical interfaces to the bundle

set interfaces ge-0/0/1 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
After commit
Run show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces ae0.
Safety note
Remove logical units from physical member ports before adding them to ae0 to avoid conflicts.
Tip
Match LACP mode and hashing on both ends for predictable behavior.

screens.title: Verifying AE and LACP
screens.subtitle: Interpreting show output and expected LACP state

narration.text: After configuring an AE bundle, you must verify that it formed correctly and that member ports are active and synchronized. The key commands are show interfaces ae0 to inspect the logical interface state and counters, and show lacp interfaces ae0 to review LACP role, timeout, activity, and per-port statistics. The chapter provides an example of expected LACP output showing actor and partner columns for each member, LACP Rx/Tx counters, and marker statistics. Use those fields to confirm both sides see compatible LACP settings and that traffic is being exchanged. A typical troubleshooting path is to check that member ports show Active or Passive states as configured, verify that partner information is present, and ensure no illegal Rx frames are reported. A common mistake to watch for is seeing no partner information — this usually indicates mode mismatch or physical connectivity issues. In a lab, observe the behaviour when you disconnect one member: the logical ae0 should stay up and counters should shift to remaining links. What metrics would you record to demonstrate that failover did not disrupt traffic? screens.title: Single Link vs Aggregated Ethernet
screens.subtitle: How AE changes availability and throughput characteristics

narration.text: Comparing a single physical link to an Aggregated Ethernet bundle clarifies the benefits AE provides. With a single link, a cable or port failure immediately takes the link and its traffic down. With AE, multiple physical links form one logical interface; if one member fails, the logical interface remains up and traffic shifts to remaining members. Throughput also changes: a single 1 Gbps link provides fixed capacity, while a bundle of two 1 Gbps links offers up to 2 Gbps aggregate bandwidth. Load balancing is different too: AE distributes flows across members using hashing so many simultaneous flows can use the aggregated capacity, whereas a single link confines all flows to one path. A common misconception is that AE guarantees perfect per-flow load sharing; hashing means some flows may remain on a single member depending on hash inputs. When designing, weigh how your traffic patterns will interact with hashing and plan minimum-links to preserve desired redundancy. To verify your design, measure throughput before and after a simulated link failure to ensure the logical interface stays up and traffic continues. Single Link vs Aggregated Ethernet means ae raises both availability and aggregate throughput, but load distribution depends on hashing and flow characteristics.. In practical terms, how ae changes availability and throughput characteristics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison takeaway
keyIdea.text: AE raises both availability and aggregate throughput, but load distribution depends on hashing and flow characteristics.

content.html:
Comparison › Single Link vs Aggregated Ethernet
Single physical link
  • Single point of failure: cable or port outage drops traffic.
  • Fixed bandwidth equal to the link speed.
  • Simpler debugging, but lower resilience.
Risk
An outage causes service disruption until the physical link is restored.
Aggregated Ethernet (AE)
  • Logical interface persists if one or more member links fail (depending on minimum-links).
  • Aggregate bandwidth equals sum of active member links.
  • Load balancing distributes flows across members using hashing.
Benefit
Higher availability and throughput; careful hashing and minimum-links choices ensure expected behavior.
Check your design
Measure flow distribution and simulate member failures to confirm that AE meets performance and availability goals under realistic traffic patterns.

screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab scenario from the chapter

Note the expected LACP counters and actor/partner states in the provided example output. A common mistake in labs is forgetting to remove IP or logical units from member ports before bundling them; ensure members are clean. After the lab, reflect: did traffic continue without interruption and did your verification commands show consistent LACP state? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Create ae0, enable LACP, add two member ports, verify formation, then test link failure to confirm continuity and observe LACP behavior.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough › Hands-on Activity: Create ae0 and test failover
Instructions summary
  1. Access the Junos CLI and enter configure mode.
  2. Create ae0 and set it to ethernet-switching trunk, assign VLANs.
  3. Enable aggregated-ether-options lacp active and set minimum-links 1.
  4. Assign ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/1 to ae0 with ether-options 802.3ad ae0.
  5. Commit, then verify show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces ae0.
  6. Disconnect one member link and observe ae0 remains up and traffic continues.
Safety note
Ensure physical members have no conflicting logical units prior to bundling to avoid configuration conflicts.
Starter template
# user@switch> configure

# Define ae0
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching interface-mode trunk
set interfaces ae0 unit 0 family ethernet-switching vlan members all
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options minimum-links 1
set interfaces ae0 aggregated-ether-options lacp active

# Add members
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 ether-options 802.3ad ae0
set interfaces ge-0/0/1 ether-options 802.3ad ae0

# commit and verify
commit and-quit
show interfaces ae0
show lacp interfaces ae0

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to retain. First, Nonstop Forwarding permits the Packet Forwarding Engine to continue forwarding using its last-known forwarding entries during a Routing Engine switchover, preventing traffic blackholing. Second, the Packet Forwarding Engine is the high-speed component that holds forwarding tables and performs forwarding independently of the Routing Engine. Third, Aggregated Ethernet bundles multiple physical links into one logical interface, providing increased bandwidth and link redundancy. Keep these three ideas clear: NSF handles control-plane transitions, the PFE is the data-plane actor, and AE addresses physical link availability. Remember to always verify behavior after configuration and consider both control-plane and link-layer resilience when designing networks. Which of these would you prioritize first for a critical uplink: enabling NSF for routing protocols, or building an AE bundle? The right answer depends on whether the primary risk is a control-plane switchover or physical link failure.

keyIdea.title: Core concepts set 1
keyIdea.text: NSF, PFE, and AE are the foundational mechanisms for data-plane continuity across control and link failures.

content.html:
Summary › Key Concepts
Nonstop Forwarding (NSF)
Allows PFE to forward on last-known table entries during RE unavailability.
Packet Forwarding Engine (PFE)
The data-plane component that holds forwarding state and forwards at line rate.
Aggregated Ethernet (AE / LAG)
Bundles multiple links into one logical interface for redundancy and aggregate bandwidth.
Summary takeaway

Combine NSF with GRES and NSR for control-plane resiliency and use AE with LACP for link-level redundancy to achieve continuous data-plane forwarding.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Operational Details
screens.subtitle: Quick operational reminders and protocol items

narration.text: These operational reminders help when you implement and troubleshoot. First, Link Aggregation Control Protocol negotiates and manages AE bundles; ensure LACP modes match and watch partner roles and activity. Second, the grace period is the window during which PFEs retain forwarding state to allow a new Routing Engine and NSR to restore adjacencies; understanding that window helps set expectations during switchover tests. Third, remember to verify both configuration and runtime state with the show commands discussed earlier, and to avoid common mistakes like leaving logical units on member ports or setting minimum-links too high. Each of these operational items is practical: LACP keeps bundles healthy, the grace period is what lets NSF bridge the gap, and verification commands provide the evidence you need that changes had the expected effect. When planning a maintenance test, sequence your checks so you can demonstrate forwarding continuity, adjacency restoration, and AE stability.

keyIdea.title: Operational checklist
keyIdea.text: Match LACP modes, understand grace periods, and always verify with show commands after configuration or tests.

content.html:
What to Remember › Key Concepts — Operational Details
Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP)
Use LACP to negotiate bundles; ensure modes and hashing match across both ends.
Grace Period
The interval PFEs retain forwarding state so NSR and the new RE can recover without disrupting traffic.
Verification commands
Use show interfaces ae0 and show lacp interfaces ae0 to confirm state, counters, and partner info.
Final takeaway

NSF and AE address two different failure domains. Use NSF for control-plane continuity and AE for link-level redundancy; verify both with targeted tests to prove data-plane continuity.
